findings.source_passage: the original Samuel must long ago have slipped his cable for the great South Sea of the other world
findings.source_locator: paragraph after the Syren passage, 'All honor to the Enderbies'
findings.why_it_matters: This is a distinctive, voice-establishing joke — the narrator's whaling idiom applied to death — and it is part of the 'All honor to the Enderbies' paragraph that also carries the phrase 'exists to the present day.' Both are erased entirely, cutting a signature piece of Melvillean wit.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the 'All honor to the Enderbies' sentence and the 'slipped his cable for the great South Sea of the other world' line verbatim; they are compact enough to fit easily.

findings.source_passage: and may my parson forget me, and the devil remember me, if I ever lose sight of it
findings.source_locator: forecastle gam paragraph, after 'solid, Saxon hospitality of that ship'
findings.why_it_matters: This oath-formula is one of the chapter's most recognizable rhetorical flourishes — a signature of the narrator's exuberant irreverence. The entire clause and the preceding 'noble, solid, Saxon hospitality' sentence are cut, erasing a voice-defining moment.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'it minds me of the noble, solid, Saxon hospitality of that ship; and may my parson forget me, and the devil remember me, if I ever lose sight of it' verbatim.

findings.source_passage: A short life to them, and a jolly death
findings.source_locator: forecastle gam paragraph, after 'every soul on board'
findings.why_it_matters: A short, epigrammatic line that is tonally distinctive and culturally quotable; its sardonic warmth is a signature of Melville's whaling-world voice. The draft skips from 'every soul on board' directly to reefing the topsails.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert 'A short life to them, and a jolly death' verbatim after the mention of all trumps on board.

findings.source_passage: Most statistical tables are parchingly dry in the reading; not so in the present case, however, where the reader is flooded with whole pipes, barrels, quarts, and gills of good gin and good cheer
findings.source_locator: paragraph immediately after the Dutch provisions list
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence is a classic example of Melville's self-conscious, ironic meta-commentary on his own digressive method; 'parchingly dry' and 'flooded with… gills' is a pointed rhetorical figure. Its loss flattens the narrator's voice at a key juncture.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the sentence after the provisions list; it is brief and carries the chapter's ironic register.

findings.source_passage: I devoted three days to the studious digesting of all this beer, beef, and bread, during which many profound thoughts were incidentally suggested to me, capable of a transcendental and Platonic application
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'At the time, I devoted three days'
findings.why_it_matters: The mock-scholarly aside about 'transcendental and Platonic application' from studying beer rations is a signature ironic digression that parodies academic method; cutting it erases the satirical register that defines this chapter.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the 'three days digesting' passage with the 'transcendental and Platonic application' phrase; the unctuous-natures observation that follows may be trimmed but this sentence must appear.

findings.source_passage: I impute it, though, to their naturally unctuous natures, being rendered still more unctuous by the nature of their vocation
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'At the time, I devoted three days'
findings.why_it_matters: 'Unctuous natures… rendered still more unctuous' is a characteristic Melvillean pun (literal fat / moral oiliness) that the critical tradition notes; its omission is a voice loss in a chapter where such wordplay is structural.
findings.suggested_fix: Include at least one sentence on the 'unctuous natures' observation to preserve the pun and the mock-ethnographic tone.

findings.source_passage: my friend Dr. Snodhead, a very learned man, professor of Low Dutch and High German in the college of Santa Claus and St. Pott's, to whom I handed the work for translation, giving him a box of sperm candles for his trouble
findings.why_it_matters: The absurd invented college name ('Santa Claus and St. Pott's') and the payment in sperm candles are pure Melvillean comedy; the draft reduces Snodhead to a brief attribution, losing the satirical invention entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the college of Santa Claus and St. Pott's and the sperm-candle fee; these details are brief but carry disproportionate voice weight.

summary: The draft achieves adequate plot compression but erases multiple high-priority voice signatures — the 'slipped his cable' death-joke, the parson-and-devil oath, 'A short life to them and a jolly death,' the mock-scholarly 'transcendental and Platonic application' passage, the 'parchingly dry' meta-commentary, and the satirically named college of Santa Claus and St. Pott's — gutting the ironic narrator's voice that is this chapter's primary content.
